Brianchon In Ellipse

GeometryCurvesConstructions
Game: This is a picture to explore: six dots sit on an oval and straight lines only brush past it at each dot.
How to play: Drag a dot along the oval, or drag a corner of the faint box to change its shape. You can also focus a dot and use the arrow keys; press Check the theorem to test what you see.
Look for the math

Drag the dots and the oval changes shape, yet the three long lines keep finding the same spot. That is the surprise behind this picture.

Lines that only just touch

At each dot there is a tangent: a line that grazes the ellipse without crossing it. The applet makes one by drawing a tangent to a circle and stretching the circle into the ellipse. In board units, with centre (cx, cy) and half-widths a, b, the tangent at dot (xA, yA) obeys (x−cx)(xA−cx)/a² + (y−cy)(yA−cy)/b² = 1. The logic test checks this at both ends of every tangent on 400 different ellipses.

Six corners and three long lines

Neighbouring tangents meet at six corners that wrap a hexagon around the ellipse. Join each pair of opposite corners: AB—DE, BC—EF and CD—FA. Brianchon's theorem says these three long lines always pass through one point, called S here. The test tried 400 shapes, including very stretched ellipses: all three lines met every time, and the point agreed with the applet's own calculation.

Why an ellipse is no harder than a circle

The cut-the-knot page says the theorem is of a projective nature, so proving it for one proper conic proves it for them all. Stretching and sliding a circle by an affine map gives a tilted ellipse while keeping tangents and intersections. The logic test makes such a map and finds that the three lines still meet; the page's claim held in every case tried.

The other side of the story

Each tangent here is the polar of the dot it touches. Turn the picture inside out — points become lines and lines become points — and Brianchon's theorem becomes Pascal's theorem about six points on a conic. That is another way to see why the oval's exact shape cannot matter. When two dots are almost neighbours their tangents are nearly parallel, so the applet refuses to draw a point for them; move them apart and the meeting point comes back.

Try dragging one dot almost onto its neighbour: the lines get close to parallel and S runs far away. Then drag it back and watch all three lines cross at one dot again.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
